summary: 哀帝崩后即位，桓温枋头之败后欲立威，诬帝不能男，废为东海王，后降海西公；太元十一年薨于吴。
summary_en: Succeeding Emperor Ai, he was deposed after Huan Wen's defeat at Fangtou — Wen, seeking to awe the court, falsely charged the emperor with impotence, degraded him to Prince of Donghai and then Duke of Haixi; he died in Wu in the 11th year of Taiyuan.

bio_md:
# 晋废帝 · 主要事迹

司马奕字延龄，成帝子，哀帝弟，封东海王。兴宁三年哀帝崩，奕即位，改元太和。废帝在位六年，无大失德；然其时桓温北伐前燕，太和四年至枋头，粮尽退军，大败而归——北伐之望绝，桓温之威受挫。

桓温素有异志，枋头之败后，名实俱损，遂思借废立以立威：太和六年十一月，温入朝，诬帝「痿疾不能男」，以太后令废帝为东海王，又降为海西公。帝被废后，温犹使人构陷，帝「深自晦匿」，杜口不谈朝事，惟以声色自晦——「海西公」遂得善终。

太元十一年，海西公薨于吴，年四十五。史家论废帝：「帝实无大过，温欲立威而废之。」东晋门阀政治，权臣可以一言废立天子，自桓温废帝始；其后桓玄篡位、刘裕禅代，皆沿此轨。废帝以一庸主之身，遭权臣之诬，虽保首领，然中国皇权之尊严，自此扫地。

> 参考：点校本《晋书》卷008《海西公纪》、卷098《桓温传》。

bio_parts_en.value:
Sima Yi, styled Yanling, was a son of Emperor Cheng and younger brother of Emperor Ai, enfeoffed Prince of Donghai. On Ai's death in the 3rd year of Xingning he took the throne, changing the era to Taihe. Six years he reigned without great fault; but in the 4th year of Taihe Huan Wen's northern expedition against Former Yan ran out of grain at Fangtou and came back in ruin — the hope of the north was gone, and Wen's prestige was wounded.

Wen, who harbored designs, sought to restore his name by deposing the emperor: in the eleventh month of the 6th year of Taihe he came to court, falsely charged the emperor with impotence — "the emperor cannot father sons" — and by the empress dowager's edict deposed him as Prince of Donghai, later reducing him to Duke of Haixi. Even in exile Wen's men came to slander him; the deposed emperor "hid himself utterly," never speaking of court affairs, hiding in music and women — and so the Duke of Haixi died in his bed.

In the 11th year of Taiyuan the Duke of Haixi died in Wu at forty-five. The historians say: "The emperor was in fact without great fault; Wen deposed him to awe the court." That a strong minister could depose an emperor on a word began with Huan Wen's act; Huan Xuan's usurpation and Liu Yu's abdication followed the same road. A mediocre sovereign done to death by calumny, he kept his life but not his throne — and the dignity of the imperial office, in Eastern Jin, was never quite the same.

> References: the punctuated critical edition of the *Jinshu*, ch. 8 ("Benji of the Duke of Haixi"), ch. 98 (biography of Huan Wen).
